posts.title: A brown bear cub explores the forest floor
posts.body: A brown bear cub stays with its mother for two to three years, and every day is a lesson. Cubs balance on fallen logs, poke through branches and test everything with nose and paws. Their small size and big curiosity make them look playful, but their mother is never far away, so keep your distance.

posts.title: A fox kit's first weeks near the den
posts.body: Fox kits are born blind in an underground den in early spring. At about four weeks old they start to venture out, staying close to the entrance on the forest floor, fluffy, brown and curious about everything. They sit and watch the world from the den's mouth among roots and fallen branches while the parents hunt. By late summer they will leave home for good.

posts.title: Arctic fox siblings play-fight in the snow
posts.body: Young arctic foxes spend their first winter testing each other in mock fights. Two littermates wrestle, snap and tumble through the snow with their mouths wide open, but nobody gets hurt: play-fighting teaches them the timing and strength they will need to hunt lemmings and defend a territory later on. Their pure white winter coats make the game almost invisible against the snowfield.

posts.title: Why black bears nap in trees
posts.body: Black bears are skilled climbers, and adults sometimes rest high up on a thick branch, legs dangling, to escape the heat or the attention of other bears. A bear lying stretched out on a tree limb in the middle of the day is not stuck; it is simply taking a nap where nothing can bother it.

posts.title: City foxes after dark
posts.body: When the shops close, urban foxes come out. In many towns they cross supermarket car parks and residential streets every night, weaving between parked cars in search of dropped food and rodents. Streetlights and headlights don't seem to bother them much. If you see one standing calmly next to a row of cars at midnight, you are looking at one of the most successful city dwellers in Europe.

posts.title: What coral reef bleaching means
posts.body: When ocean water stays too warm for too long, corals expel the tiny algae living in their tissues. Without them the coral turns white and starts to starve. Bleached reefs can recover if temperatures fall quickly, but repeated marine heatwaves are leaving less and less time for the reef to heal.

posts.title: How the Dalmatian gets its spots
posts.body: Dalmatian puppies are born pure white; their famous black or liver spots only appear after about two weeks. Every Dalmatian's pattern is unique. Bred as carriage dogs that ran alongside horses, Dalmatians are athletic, high-energy dogs with short, sleek white coats that need very little grooming but shed all year round.

posts.title: Deer on misty roads at dawn
posts.body: Early morning fog and forest roads are a dangerous mix. Deer are most active at dawn, and in the mist a spotted deer standing on the asphalt can appear out of nowhere. Slow down on roads that cut through woodland, watch the verges, and remember that where one deer crosses, others often follow.

posts.title: How emperor penguins huddle through the Antarctic winter
posts.body: Through the Antarctic winter, male emperor penguins incubate a single egg on their feet for more than two months, without eating. To survive winds of 200 km/h and temperatures below minus 40, thousands of them press together in a huddle, taking turns on the cold outer edge before shuffling back into the warm centre.

posts.title: Fallow deer in a summer meadow
posts.body: Fallow deer are easy to recognise: a spotted coat in summer and, in the males, broad palmate antlers. A buck grazing in a meadow full of yellow wildflowers will often stop to groom, twisting its head round to scratch its back with its antlers. Many parks in Europe keep fallow deer, which were spread across the continent by the Normans and the Romans.

posts.title: The fennec fox and its giant ears
posts.body: The fennec fox is the smallest fox in the world, a pale sand-coloured desert animal from the Sahara. Its enormous ears, up to 15 cm long, radiate heat and let it hear insects moving under the sand. Thick fur on the soles of its feet protects it from the burning dunes, and it can go for long periods without drinking, getting water from its food.

posts.title: Bandana style for golden retrievers
posts.body: A bandana is the easiest accessory for a dog: light, cheap and easy to wash. Blue looks great against a golden retriever's warm golden coat. Tie it loosely enough to fit two fingers underneath, and take it off for rough play. On a sunny afternoon in the garden, a happy retriever in a fresh bandana is the best photo you'll take all week.

posts.title: Inside a wolf's mouth
posts.body: A wolf has 42 teeth, including four long canines built to grip struggling prey and carnassial teeth that shear meat like scissors. The best time to see them is during a big yawn, when the jaws open wide and the whole set of sharp teeth and the long tongue are on display. A yawn is also social: in a pack, yawns can be contagious, just like in people.

posts.title: Keeping indoor cats busy
posts.body: Indoor cats get bored, and a bored cat scratches furniture and knocks things off shelves. Give your cat climbing shelves, a scratching post and short play sessions with a feather wand twice a day. Puzzle feeders turn dinner into a hunt, and a window perch with a view of the birds outside can keep a cat entertained for hours.

posts.title: Moose, giants of the boreal forest
posts.body: The moose is the largest member of the deer family, standing over two metres at the shoulder. Bulls grow enormous flat, shovel-shaped antlers, and both sexes have a long overhanging muzzle and a flap of skin called a bell hanging from the throat. In summer moose wade into lakes and ponds to feed on water plants, sometimes dipping their whole head under the surface.

posts.title: Polar bears hunting seals on the sea ice
posts.body: Polar bears depend on sea ice. They wait for hours beside a breathing hole in the frozen Arctic Ocean, then haul out a ringed seal with one swipe. Their white fur, black skin and thick fat keep them warm in temperatures far below freezing, and huge furry paws spread their weight on thin ice. As the ice melts earlier each spring, the hunting season is getting shorter.

posts.title: Raising a Siberian husky puppy
posts.body: Siberian husky puppies are bright, stubborn and full of energy, with those famous blue eyes already visible at a few weeks old. Start training early, give them plenty of time outdoors on grass, and be ready for escape attempts: young huskies are born explorers. Socialise them with people and other dogs before they are four months old.

posts.title: Red deer in a winter herd
posts.body: In winter red deer gather in larger herds in forest clearings, where the trees give shelter from wind and falling snow. A big stag with a full set of antlers often stands among the hinds and younger animals. Together they find food under the snow and keep watch for danger.

posts.title: Small dog, big energy: the Shih Tzu puppy
posts.body: Don't let the size fool you. A Shih Tzu puppy can sprint across a lawn with its ears flapping and tongue out, then collapse for a nap five minutes later. These little brown and white dogs were bred as companions, but they still need short bursts of play every day. A safe grassy field is the perfect place for puppy zoomies.

posts.title: Sourdough starter basics
posts.body: A sourdough starter is just flour and water colonised by wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria. Feed it equal weights of flour and water once a day, keep it somewhere warm, and after a week it should double within a few hours of feeding. That's when it is ready to raise your first loaf of bread.

posts.title: The behavior of red foxes
posts.body: Red foxes are solitary hunters for most of the year. They patrol a home range of a few square kilometres, marking it with scent, and do most of their hunting at dawn and dusk. Their signature move is the mousing pounce: a fox listens for a vole moving under grass or snow, leaps high, and drops on it nose-first. In spring the family comes together, and both parents bring food to the cubs at the den. Red foxes are opportunists, eating rodents, rabbits, birds, insects, berries and our leftovers, which is why they thrive from farmland to city centres.

posts.title: The white wolves of the Arctic
posts.body: The arctic wolf is a subspecies of the grey wolf that lives in the High Arctic of Canada and Greenland. Its thick white coat hides it against snow and ice. Arctic wolves are a little smaller than their southern relatives, with shorter ears and muzzles that lose less heat. Seen walking along the edge of a wood, a white wolf looks almost ghostly.

posts.title: Vulpes vulpes: an adaptable survivor in European cities
posts.body: Few wild mammals have adapted to European cities as well as Vulpes vulpes. Once a shy hunter of farmland and woodland edges, Vulpes vulpes now raises its young under garden sheds in London, Zurich and Berlin. Its diet is famously flexible: earthworms after rain, rats, fallen fruit and whatever people leave out. City individuals are most active at dusk and through the night, travelling along railway lines and back gardens. Researchers tracking them with GPS collars find small, overlapping territories and surprisingly bold behaviour around people, a sign of how quickly a wild species can learn to share our streets.

posts.title: What wolves carry home
posts.body: After a kill, a wolf doesn't always eat on the spot. It often tears off a piece of meat and carries it in its jaws back through the forest, to cache it for later or to feed pups and pack mates at the rendezvous site. On an autumn trail you might see a grey wolf trotting purposefully with a mouthful of prey: the pack's supply line in action.

posts.title: Wild fox species of the northern hemisphere
posts.body: The northern hemisphere is home to several wild fox species. The red fox has the widest range of any wild carnivore, from Arctic tundra to deserts. The arctic fox survives temperatures far below freezing thanks to its thick white winter coat, while the swift fox and kit fox are small prairie and desert specialists. The grey fox of North America can even climb trees. All of them are lightly built, bushy-tailed hunters of small prey.

posts.title: Wolves at rest together
posts.body: Wolves spend a surprising amount of the day doing nothing. Pack members rest close together, lying or sitting side by side, which strengthens their bonds. In wildlife parks, wolves often choose a raised wooden platform among green foliage as their favourite lookout and lounging spot, keeping an eye on visitors while they doze.
